title: Wait Queue
summary:
A wait queue is the **holding area for work that cannot run yet**: waiting for a free worker, a lock, a rate-limit token, a dependency, or a scheduled time. It is not extra capacity. It converts a temporary excess of demand into **waiting time**, so the real design questions are how long, how many, in what order, and what happens to those who have waited too long.

- **Size and Little's law.** The wait for a newcomer is about `queue length / service rate`. At 100 tasks/s, a queue of 600 means 6 s. If clients give up after 2 s, anything beyond 200 queued items is doomed. **Bound the queue** (reject or shed the excess); an unbounded queue under sustained overload only grows the delay ([load shedding](#/sd/f/load-shedding), [concurrency limiter](#/sd/f/concurrency-limiter)).
- **Order.** FIFO is fair and predictable. A priority queue serves important work first but needs aging ([prioritized scheduling](#/sd/f/prioritized-scheduling)). When overloaded with deadlines, **LIFO** (newest first) maximizes requests answered in time, and is often used only when the queue is long.
- **Staleness.** Store each item's deadline and **check it at dequeue**; drop expired items instead of running them.
- **Blocking vs async.** A blocked thread per waiter is expensive; a queue of callbacks or promises is not.
- **Visibility.** Alert on queue age, not only length: age is what users feel.
- **Delay queues** hold items until a time, ordered by due time ([trigger-based invocation](#/sd/f/trigger-based-invocation)); the moving of items from a wait queue into a running set is the [wait / running queues](#/sd/f/wait-running-queues) model.

drills.q: A worker pool serves 100 tasks per second. Clients abandon a request after 2 seconds. What is the largest queue length that still lets a newly enqueued task start within the 2-second deadline (ignore its own service time)?
drills.explain: Wait = length / rate, so length = rate x deadline = 100 x 2 = 200. Beyond that, new arrivals are admitted only to be abandoned. A bounded queue of about 200 (or less) makes that explicit by rejecting the rest.

drills.q: Arrivals are 120 tasks/s and capacity is 100 tasks/s, sustained, with an unbounded FIFO queue. What happens?
options: The queue stabilizes, since the excess is only 20/s
The queue grows by 20 tasks every second, so waiting time rises without bound (1,200 queued and a 12 s wait after a minute), and memory use grows too
Throughput rises to 120/s to match demand
Nothing visible until memory runs out, because latency is unaffected
drills.explain: A queue only absorbs bursts. When average demand exceeds capacity, the backlog grows linearly. Waiting time = backlog / 100, so latency climbs from the first second.

drills.q: A worker dequeues a task whose caller deadline passed 3 seconds ago. What should it do?
options: Run it, since the work has been accepted
Discard it (optionally recording a metric); nobody is waiting, and running it delays tasks that still matter
Requeue it at the back of the line
Run it twice to be safe
drills.explain: Checking deadlines at dequeue is the cheapest form of load shedding. Without it, a backlog of dead requests keeps the system busy long after the cause of the overload has gone.

drills.q: A long queue builds under a surge. Almost every request has a 1 s deadline, and the oldest queued items are already 5 s old. Which dequeue order answers the most requests in time?
options: FIFO, since it is the fairest
LIFO (newest first), at least while the queue is long, with expired items discarded
drills.explain: The old items have already expired, so serving them first wastes capacity. Serving the newest first answers those whose clients are still waiting, trading fairness for goodput until the queue drains.

drills.q: Put the life of a request in a bounded wait queue in order.
items: The request arrives and the queue is checked for room
If the queue is full, it is rejected immediately (e.g. 503)
Otherwise it is enqueued together with its deadline
A worker slot frees up and the next item is dequeued
The deadline is checked: expired items are dropped, live ones run
drills.explain: Rejecting at arrival bounds the delay of everything admitted, and the second deadline check at dequeue handles those that expired while waiting.
